title: Weekly Mining Plan
body: When the bi-weekly plan isn't cross-checked against what's actually running, a fault like EX-123's stays written out at 0% for four straight decks with no recovery date while another document shows it back in service — and Spatial Compliance misses (82-89% against 100%) sit unexplained for months because nobody re-raises them. The plan is only useful if you read it against reality, not on its own.
keyPoints: The deck has three layers — retrospective, equipment availability grid, and forward schedule. Don't sequence off the forward numbers alone; check the retrospective for what actually happened last week first.

Treat every 0% or "written out" line on the availability grid as unverified until you check it against the current fleet/actuals report. This operation has run equipment write-outs and recovery dates that flatly contradict each other for weeks at a time.

The chronic gap here isn't availability, it's utilization — machines have repeatedly shown up available above plan while UA/use tracked below plan. That means idle and queue time on shift is the lever, not chasing more uptime.

Six focus items repeat deck after deck: spillage/overspill cleanup, dust, near-miss reporting, Stage 4D/Stage 6 simultaneous ops, fatigue management, hot-season prep. Recurring on the deck means unresolved on the ground — don't treat them as boilerplate.

A grade or compliance miss that goes unexplained once tends to stay unexplained — one Spatial Compliance gap sat open from early June to late July with no root cause because nobody owned the follow-up.
apply: Before locking in loading sequence or truck allocation, check whether any excavator or drill rig on today's roster is listed at 0% in the current bi-weekly plan but shows as running in the fleet availability report — that exact mismatch has cost this site planning accuracy multiple times this year.
